extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, writers, scholars, and educated readers interested in standards of prose and national literary character
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and critical criteria for judging and producing prose and literature: what qualities (style, ideas, form, tone) make writing classical, provincial, or great; and what role institutions (academies) play in shaping standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy (genius) and freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Energy is the most essential part of genius; 'what that energy ... above everything demands and insists upon, is freedom; entire independence of all authority, prescription, and routine, — the fullest room to expand as it will.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive: Energy enables poetry and great science (Shakspeare, Newton). Anti-pattern: excessive institutional control/rigidity can 'embarrass energy and inventive genius' and thus obstruct creative heights. Aim to protect independence and room for imaginative expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness of mind and flexibility of intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Openness of mind and flexibility of intelligence are essential intellectual qualities (noted as characteristic of the French), causing deference to standards higher than one's habitual standard and promoting adoption of 'measure and order' in thought and expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive: Quick, open, sensitive intelligence is readiest to accept higher standards and produce communicable forms. Institutions like academies propagate these qualities. Anti-pattern: lack of flexibility produces crude, hap-hazard, or provincial work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form, method, precision, proportions, relations of parts to whole
rubrics_metrics.description: The form, the method of evolution, the precision, the proportions, the relations of the parts to the whole in an intellectual work depend mainly on quickness and flexibility of intelligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are technical requisites especially vital in prose: ensure coherent structure, rigorous method, precise expression, balanced proportions and clear relations among parts. Failure shows as disorder, crudeness, and blundering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness, correctness, and propriety in thinking and speaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions and cultivated critical opinion aim at 'clearness, correctness, and propriety in thinking and speaking.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for intellectual and linguistic correctness and transparent argumentation. These are standards academies enforce; lack of them leads to poor reference works, bad translations, and diminished credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educated opinion / centralised critical authority ('sovereign organ of opinion')
rubrics_metrics.description: A body like the French Academy 'sets standards ... and creates ... a force of educated opinion, checking and rebuking those who fall below these standards.' It serves as 'a sort of centre and rallying-point' for taste and tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefit: raises baseline quality of journeyman literature, reference works, and scholarship; provides checks against charlatanism and eccentricity. Anti-pattern: absence of such a centre produces scattered minorities unable to enforce standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid provinciality; attain the 'platform' of classical culture
rubrics_metrics.description: In the bulk of intellectual work where there is no centre there is 'a note of provinciality.' Getting rid of provinciality is 'a certain stage of culture' — the platform where 'the best and highest intellectual work can be said fairly to begin.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive: aim for work that belongs to the 'centre' (classical), not merely local or parochial preoccupations. Anti-patterns: narrow localism, exaggerated partisanship, and works that display remoteness from widely recognised standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urbanity (tone): persuasion, politeness, and urbane judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Urbanity is 'the tone of the city, of the centre' — a style that 'always aims at a spiritual and intellectual effect' and 'never disjoins banter itself from politeness, from felicity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a persuasive, urbane tone over the aggressive, eruptive provincial tone. Avoid style that 'makes war' rather than persuades; cultivate graciousness, nuance, and measured banter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical (Attic) prose: simplicity, measure, and just style
rubrics_metrics.description: The true prose is described as 'Attic prose'—prose without the note of provinciality: classical, with simplicity, measure, and propriety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for clarity, restraint, and balanced rhetorical resources. Anti-patterns: Asiatic/provincial prose that is 'barbarously rich and overloaded' or extravagantly ornate (examples given in Burke's excesses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and depth of ideas (matter), not mere stylistic polish
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer must have 'ideas of the first order' on his subject; style alone is insufficient—Addison's example: perfect style but 'the idea expressed is perfectly trite and barren.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive to combine profound, novel thought with sound expression. The 'true classic' expresses new and profound ideas in a perfectly sound and classical style. Anti-pattern: polished form with commonplace matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision of style and communicability of intellectual elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The elements of intelligence (form, precision, method) are 'really most communicable from [a work], which can most be learned and adopted from it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce prose whose method and precision can be learned by readers; favor transmissible intellectual qualities. Institutions help propagate these communicable elements widely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthographical and linguistic correctness; avoid 'freaks' in language
rubrics_metrics.description: Small linguistic 'freaks' (orthographical oddities) 'tend to impair the power and beauty of language' and spread the notion that there is no high correct standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain standard orthography and conventional usage (example: The Times' former spelling 'diocess' criticised). Anti-pattern: indulgence in odd spellings or willful linguistic eccentricities that set bad examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality control for reference works and translations
rubrics_metrics.description: English books of reference and translations are judged inferior to French/German ones; without a centre, 'journeyman-work of literature ... is so much worse done here than it is in France.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For scholarly and utility publications ensure high editorial standards, reliable scholarship, and critical review. Anti-patterns: sloppiness in reference material and careless translations that make readers prefer foreign works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order and balance of ideas; avoid giving one idea excessive prominence
rubrics_metrics.description: The provincial spirit 'gives one idea too much prominence at the expense of others; it orders its ideas amiss; it is hurried away by fancies; it likes and dislikes too passionately, too exclusively.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure arguments and presentations to balance multiple relevant ideas; avoid monomania, hysterical admiration or foaming disapprobation. Aim for lucidity and measured judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid newspaper-style short, highly charged, heavy-shot prose for intellectual work
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspaper writing tendencies—'short, highly-charged, heavy-shotted articles' and resolute avoidance of shades and distinctions—are bad food for the provincial spirit and injurious to nuanced intellectual discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For serious intellectual and literary work prefer sustained, nuanced argumentation to punchy, sensationalist brevity. Anti-pattern: adopting journalistic partisanship and one-sided polemics in literary criticism.
